fields.title: What Codes Mean
fields.keyTakeaway: A response code tells whether a retry will help and whether the user can fix the situation themselves — and these are two different things that should look different on the screen.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: In the logs: 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429, and 503. All of them are "errors", but they are different — and mean completely different things to the user.
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: A product where all errors look like "something went wrong" loses users out of the blue. Half of these situations can be fixed by the person themselves in five seconds if they are told what exactly is wrong. Categorizing errors by meaning is the PM's job, because it is a question of what the person should do next.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: The first digit sets the family and already carries the main meaning.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **2xx — success.** `200` has result, `201` created, `204` done, nothing to respond with.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **4xx — failure, cause is on the requester's side.** Retrying the same request will not help: something must be changed.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **5xx — failure, cause is on our side.** The request might have been correct. A retry could help.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: Key codes and what they mean for a person:
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/0/2: App bug, not user error. "Something went wrong", log as defect
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/1/2: Session expired — send to login, preserving context
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/2/2: "You do not have access". Sending to login is pointless
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/3/2: "Product is no longer available" — specifically, not "error"
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/4/2: "Order already cancelled", "this phone number is taken"
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/5/2: Form field error — show next to the field
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/6/2: "Too fast, try again in a minute"
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/7/2: "We are already fixing it". Retrying makes sense
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/8/1: Service unavailable or did not respond
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/8/2: Temporary — retry makes sense, show ability to wait
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: The distinction between `401` and `403` is the most common confusion, and it is visible to the user: on `403`, suggesting to log in again leads to an infinite loop.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: Separately, there is a [[timeout|timeout]] — no response at all. This is not a code, but the absence of one, and it represents the worst of states: **we do not know whether the operation happened or not.** The next lesson covers this.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Analysis of the checkout screen before and after.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: Before: a single message "Failed to place order. Try again" for all cases. Retry rate 34%, of which 11% were successful.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: *`409` item out of stock* — "Milk is no longer available in this store", "Remove and continue" button. Retrying is pointless, and we state that. *`422` address out of delivery zone* — message by the address field, suggestion to choose another store. *`402` from payment provider, insufficient funds* — "Bank declined payment", suggestion for another card. *`503`* — "We are overloaded, please wait a minute", automatic retry after 30 seconds.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: The share of successful retries grew to 61%, and support tickets regarding checkout dropped by almost half. Not a single technical fix — only parsing what was already arriving.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Not all APIs follow code semantics: there are services that return `200` with an error text inside. This is a defect in their contract, and on our side it is handled by parsing the response body.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: A response code tells whether a retry will help and whether the user can fix the situation themselves — and these are two different things that should look different on the screen.
